title: Combinations of solids
examples: If I melt a cube and recast it into spheres, how do I find the number of spheres?
What is the key principle when converting one solid shape to another?
Do I need to worry about the material shrinking when I melt it?

explain.say: Today we are looking at melting and recasting solids. This means changing one shape into another.
The most important rule here is that the total volume stays the same. Volume does not change during this process.

items: Recast it into a new shape

explain.say: We find the volume of the original solid first. Then we find the volume of the new shape.
To find the number of new shapes, you divide the total starting volume by the volume of one new shape.
For example, if you melt a block with a volume of one hundred eighty pi cubic metres. And one small sphere has a volume of pi cubic metres. You can make one hundred eighty spheres.

faq.q: Does the material change when I melt it?
faq.a: No, the material itself does not change. Only its shape changes when it melts and is recast.
asks: Is the material always the same?

faq.q: Do I have to worry about the density changing?
faq.a: No, for these problems, you can assume that the density remains constant throughout the melting and recasting process.
asks: Do I need to use density calculations?

faq.q: If the original shape is complex, how do I find its volume?
faq.a: You must break the complex shape down into simpler shapes like cubes, cylinders, or spheres to find the total volume.
asks: What if the shape is weird?
How do I find the volume of a combined shape?

faq.q: Should I use pi in my final answer or use a decimal value?
faq.a: It is best practice to keep pi in your answer until the very last step, unless the question tells you to round to a specific decimal place.
asks: When should I calculate the final number?

faq.q: What if the total volume is less than the volume of one new shape?
faq.a: If the total volume is less than the volume of one new shape, you can make zero complete new shapes.
asks: Can I make a partial shape?

facts: Volume is a measure of the three-dimensional space an object occupies.
When melting and recasting, the total volume remains constant.
The volume of a cylinder is calculated by pi times radius squared times height.
The volume of a sphere is four pi over three times the radius cubed.

quiz.say: A metal block has a volume of 36 pi cubic metres. If one small sphere has a volume of pi cubic metres, how many spheres can be made?
quiz.why: You divide the total volume by the volume of one sphere, which gives you thirty-six spheres.

wrong.0: This mistake happens when students confuse division with squaring the number.
wrong.2: This might be a common mistake if you incorrectly add the volumes together instead of dividing.
wrong.3: This incorrectly keeps pi in the answer when the units suggest a whole number count.

quiz.say: A metal object has a volume of 150 cubic centimetres. If you recast it into small cubes, and each cube has a volume of 6 cubic centimetres, how many cubes can you form?
quiz.why: You divide the total volume by the volume of one small cube to find the total count.

wrong.0: This happens if you add the volumes together by mistake.
wrong.2: This is a common error when students subtract the volumes instead of dividing them.
wrong.3: This mistake occurs if you multiply the two volumes together by mistake.

quiz.say: A large cylinder of metal has a volume of 750 pi cubic centimetres. If you melt it and recast it into small spheres, each with a volume of 15 pi cubic centimetres, how many spheres can you make?
quiz.why: You divide the total volume by the small sphere's volume, which cancels out pi, leaving fifty.

wrong.1: This mistake incorrectly assumes the final answer must include pi units.
wrong.2: This happens if you subtract the volumes instead of dividing them.
wrong.3: This mistake occurs if you multiply the two volumes together.
